title: Near Misses
briefing: Valtren's yard safety record looks excellent: one reportable injury in two years. Grace Mbeki, Head of Health and Safety, is not convinced. Near-miss reports dropped by 70% after supervisors' bonuses were linked to 'incident-free months'.
She has asked the risk team to look at the data and tell the Operations Board what it really says.

context.text: The A-road collision is still under investigation. The board is sensitive to anything that looks like hidden risk.
Your control test on data loggers impressed Ruth Adeyemi; she has told Grace you can be trusted with awkward findings.

evidence.title: Near-miss reports by quarter
body: Yard movements per quarter were stable at about 52,000 throughout.

evidence.title: Supervisor bonus scheme (extract)
evidence.body: Supervisors receive 1,500 for each 'incident-free month' at their depot. Near misses logged on the system count as incidents for this purpose.

evidence.title: Sample CCTV review (Health and Safety)
evidence.body: A review of 20 random yard shifts after the scheme started found 17 events that met the near-miss definition (reversing without a banksman, pedestrians in vehicle lanes). Two of them were logged.

evidence.title: Injury statistics
evidence.body: One reportable injury in 24 months (a forklift strike, month 22). Industry benchmark for comparable yards: about one per 400,000 movements.

questions.prompt: What does the fall in near-miss reports most likely show?

options.label: Under-reporting caused by the bonus scheme, not safer yards
options.feedback: Activity was flat, CCTV shows near misses still happening, and the drop starts exactly when the bonus did.

options.label: Safer yards: the bonus focused supervisors on safety, and the injury rate supports that
options.feedback: The CCTV sample contradicts this: 17 near misses in 20 shifts, 2 logged.

options.label: Normal variation: near-miss reporting fluctuates, and two years is too short to judge
options.feedback: A 70% step change at a known date, with stable activity, is not noise.

questions.prompt: Using the CCTV sample, roughly what share of near misses now gets reported?
questions.explanation: 2 / 17 = 12%. A small sample, so quote it as an indication.

mistakes.feedback: That is the share of shifts with events, not the reporting rate.
Reports fell by 70%; that does not tell you the reporting rate.

questions.prompt: How do you rate near-miss reporting as a detective control today?

options.label: Ineffective: the incentive punishes the behaviour the control depends on
options.feedback: A control that depends on self-reporting fails when reporting is penalised.

options.label: Effective: reports are fewer because supervisors now manage hazards before they become events
Partially effective: serious events are still being reported, which is what matters most
options.feedback: 12% capture is not partially effective for a safety control.

questions.prompt: What do you recommend to the Operations Board? Your authority is 25,000.

options.label: Stop counting near misses against the bonus, reward good reporting, and sample CCTV monthly
options.feedback: Removes the perverse incentive and adds an independent detective control.

options.label: Audit each depot's CCTV and discipline supervisors whose depots are found to under-report
options.feedback: The scheme created the behaviour; punishing people for responding to it will drive reporting further underground.

options.label: Keep the scheme: injuries are better than the industry benchmark, which is the outcome that counts
options.feedback: One injury in 24 months is too few events to prove safety, and the leading indicator is broken.

schedules.description: A pedestrian is struck by a reversing trailer in the Northgate yard

questions.prompt: The Operations Director designed the bonus scheme and is proud of it. How do you handle him before the board?

options.label: Brief him privately first with the data, acknowledge the scheme's intent, and agree a joint recommendation
options.feedback: No surprises in the board room, and the owner of the problem co-owns the fix.

options.label: Present the data at the board as it stands, without a pre-brief, so the evidence is judged on its merits
options.feedback: Surprising a director in public makes him defend the scheme instead of fixing it.

options.label: Recommend changes to reporting but leave the bonus scheme itself out of the paper
options.feedback: Omitting the root cause leaves the board unable to fix it.

lesson: Low incident numbers can mean hidden risk. Incentives shape reporting: check whether a control relies on people reporting against their own interest.
